\(PBS\)

*The Marlow Murder Club* is not going anywhere anytime soon\. The *Masterpiece* series has been renewed for a six-episode third season ahead of its second season return in August\.

Samantha Bond, Jo Martin, Cara Horgan, Natalie Dew, Holli Dempsey, Phill Langhorne, and Tijan Sarr star in the mystery series based on the novels by Robert Thorogood\.

PBS shared the following about season three:

> “Now an established part of newly promoted DI Tanika Malik’s \(Natalie Dew\) crime-solving team, retired archaeologist Judith Potts \(Samantha Bond\), dog walker Suzie Harris \(Jo Martin\) and vicar’s wife Becks Starling \(Cara Horgan\) are back and bringing their unconventional methods to a string of high-profile murders\.
> 
> From the sudden death of the nicest man in Marlow, the town’s beloved mayor, to a celebrity chef found dead at the launch of his cookbook with half the town in attendance, the team will be working under the watchful eye of the Marlow community\. They’ll also be called to action at a university reunion in an eerie manor house where in a surprising twist, Becks finds herself amongst the suspects\. Could this case threaten our amateur sleuths’ roles as civilian advisors?”

Susanne Simpson, executive producer of MASTERPIECE on PBS, spoke about the renewal\. She said, “It’s a thrill to bring a third season of *The Marlow Murder Club* to our US audience\. I know our viewers are looking forward to more of the heart and humor that makes this series so special\.”

The premiere date for season three will be announced later\. Season two premieres on **August 24th**\.

What do you think? Did you watch season one of this Masterpiece series? Do you plan to watch seasons two and three?

BOYD COUNTY, Ky\. \(WSAZ\) - Construction crews are shaping what will soon be a quarter horse racing track at Sandy’s Racing and Gaming\.

Sandy’s Racing and Gaming in Boyd County is picking up steam on its Sandy Ridge Racetrack, which is set to host its first quarter horse races in August\. Right now, crews are preparing for their “photo finish\.”

Sandy’s general manager Sara Ann Marlow said the project marks a milestone for the facility and the community\.

“Right now, crews are focused on building the oval track and racing surface, developing barns, a paddock area and operation area, finalizing guest spaces and infrastructures,” Marlow said\. “It’s being designed as a full entertainment destination, not a temporary add on\.”

The current focus is getting the track ready in time for Sandy’s inaugural quarter horse races in August\. Preparation includes building new barns, paddocks, seats and fan amenities\.

Quarter horses are known for their short, high-speed sprints\.

“Guests can expect something completely new for the region\. Fast-paced, high-energy racing paired with an entertainment experience,” Marlow said\. “Quarter horse races are short, explosive sprints\. Think seconds, not minutes\.”

Beyond the track itself, the project is expected to boost tourism and create new jobs\.

“The goal is simple, come for the races, stay for a full night out,” Marlow said\.

If all goes as planned, the gates will open in August\.

“Bottom line, it positions Boyd County as a destination, not a pass through,” Marlow said\.

BUTLER TWP, Ohio \(WDTN\) — The man accused of shooting and killing four people in a Butler Township neighborhood earlier this month is facing nine additional charges\.

Thirty-nine-year-old Stephen Marlow was originally charged with eight counts of aggravated murder, four counts of aggravated burglary and one count of having weapons under disability\.

Court records filed Tuesday, August 23 show that Marlow now faces four additional counts of aggravated murder \(prior calculation/design\), four additional counts of aggravated burglary and one count of tampering with evidence\.

The victims of the shooting were identified as 82-year-old Clyde Knox, 78-year-old Eva Knox, 41-year-old Sarah Anderson and her 15-year-old daughter Kayla\.

***Warning: Extremely Graphic Content Ahead***

Court documents state that on Friday, August 5 at approximately 11:35 a\.m\., Marlow walked into an open, attached garage on Hardwicke Place and shot Sarah Anderson multiple times\. He then walked into the home, located Kayla Anderson in the kitchen, and fatally shot her several times\. As he walked back out into the garage, he noticed that Sarah was still moving\. He then fired a single shot in the back of her head, killing her\.

A home security camera located in the Anderson’s garage captured and depicted Marlow shooting Sarah, enter the home to murder Kayla, then exit the home approximately 12 seconds later to murder Sarah\.

A witness watched Marlow exit the garage and spoke to him\. The witness stated that Marlow holstered a gun and threatened him\. The witness later was able to positively identify Marlow in a photo lineup\.

After murdering Sarah and Kayla Anderson, Marlow entered a detached garage on the same street near the Anderson residence, where he fatally shot Clyde and Eva Knox\.

A witness stated that he heard gunshots and looked out the window to see Marlow getting into a white Ford SUV\. The witness took note of the license plate number and immediately went to check on his neighbors, Clyde and Eva Knox, finding them deceased in the garage\.

Marlow then fled the scene in a white Ford SUV and drove to his home address where he lived with his parents on Haverstraw Avenue\.

A search warrant was later executed on the Haverstraw Avenue residence\. During that search, a manifesto was found on a computer believed to be Marlow’s\.

The manifesto was typed out, and in it, Marlow states his name, address and life story\. He spoke of conspiracy theories and believing that his neighbors were terrorists engaged in the mind control of others\. He said that he believed it to be one of the greatest crimes against humanity in history\. In addition, crews found “bomb-making” criteria in his Internet search history\.

Later in the evening, Marlow released a pre-recorded video stating that he was going to launch, “The first counterattack against mind control in history”\. He specified that it would not be an active shooter incident, but instead he would target and “execute” only those responsible\. He expressed his desire to encourage other “targeted individuals” and made it clear that this was a cause he was prepared to die for\.

On August 6, it was discovered that Stephen had a storage unit located on North Dixie Drive\. Surveillance shows Marlow entering the property on the day of the incident at 11:12 a\.m\. and exiting the unit at 11:27 a\.m\., just minutes before the murders took place\.

A search warrant was executed on his storage unit\. Inside, crews located an empty gun case that would normally store an AR-15 style rifle, handgun and rifle ammunition, a manual for an AR-15 high-capacity drum magazine, an empty box for a long-range rifle scope, rifle magazines that loaded and empty, and some writings on warfare\.

Later in the evening on August 6, Marlow was located and arrested in Lawrence, Kansas, where he was interviewed by the FBI\. During that interview, Marlow stated that he knew he could not possess any firearms due to his prior aggravated burglary charge\. He deliberately circumvented this by traveling to Kentucky and meeting a private seller to obtain the firearms\.

Marlow admitted that his motive for buying the firearms was to carry out his attack against the individuals who he believed to be a part of this “terrorist cell”\. He stated that he stored the firearms in his storage unit to conceal them from his mother until the day of the murders\.

On August 17, Marlow was extradited back to Ohio\. On the way back, he was interviewed by police\. He asked if his manifesto was received and repeated much of the same information that was provided during the initial interview\.

When asked if he had additional targets, Marlow said that he did not want to talk about it on camera\. When asked for a reason for his killings, Marlow stated that it was an act of self-defense to protect his family, and for the purpose of “exposure”\.

According to police, when asked how he felt about everything, he said something to the effect of, “For me, it was an easy decision\.”

Marlow remains booked in the Montgomery County Jail\. His next court date has not been scheduled\.

# Julius Marlow Taps AFL’s Isaac Quaynor To Front New Campaign

*Australian men’s footwear brand Julius Marlow unveiled AFL player Isaac Quaynor as brand ambassador and the face of its new ‘Own The Moment’ campaign\. *

Quaynor champions a “Footy, Fashion, and Fragrance” ethos, swapping the MCG turf for the Melbourne Fashion Festival runway\. Quaynor represents a new generation of athletes who treat personal style as an extension of who they are beyond sport\.

“For me, style has always been an extension of who I am outside of footy\. Changing out of my boots after a game is the ultimate reset, and ‘Own The Moment’ really speaks to taking confidence into whatever room you step into\. Julius Marlow is an iconic Melbourne brand, and I’m pumped to lead this new chapter with them,” said Quaynor\.

The campaign also debuted Julius Marlow’s Investment Collection: a range combining the brand’s signature comfort technology with refined silhouettes built for occasion dressing\. Key styles include the Coda and Code dress shoes, as well as the Colt Chelsea Boot\.

“Isaac embodies everything this new chapter of Julius Marlow is about\. He’s an incredible athlete, but off the field, he brings a modern, confident, and ambitious approach to personal style that really resonates with Australian men\. It’s exactly what we wanted our ‘Own the Moment’ campaign to capture – Julius Marlow showing up for men in the moments that matter\. Partnering with someone who genuinely lives that, we’re able to showcase an elevated range men can rely on, season after season,” head of Julius Marlow Charlotte MacIntyre said\.

To celebrate the partnership and the launch of the Investment Collection, Julius Marlow will host an exclusive, invite-only event in Melbourne on Wednesday 5th August\.

Bringing together Quaynor, close friends, media and lifestyle influencers, the night will showcase the collection’s style in an environment where sporting culture meets fashion\.

The ‘Own The Moment’ campaign launched today\.

# Resurfaced audio captures Abdul El-Sayed downplaying terrorist attack on Michigan synagogue

August 9, 2026

Audio from a Michigan political figure dismissing a terrorist attack on a synagogue as a case of \"hurt people hurt people\" has resurfaced, drawing fresh scrutiny over how the incident's Hezbollah connections were minimized\.

Breitbart Editor-in-Chief Alex Marlow spotlighted the story on his Wednesday broadcast, laying out what he described as a disturbing chain: the individual at the center of a Michigan attack on a synagogue had a brother who was, as Marlow reported, a Hezbollah member killed by Israel in Lebanon\. That family connection, Marlow argued, was not incidental, it was the motive\. And Abdul El-Sayed's response amounted to explaining it away\.

The core issue is straightforward: a terrorist attack took place against a Michigan synagogue, and resurfaced audio shows El-Sayed treating the attacker's grievance, the death of a Hezbollah-tied brother at the hands of Israel, as a kind of psychological explanation rather than a red flag\. The phrase attributed to the attacker's framing: \"hurt people hurt people\.\" El-Sayed, rather than condemning the act in clear terms, reportedly echoed that logic\.

## Marlow connects the Hezbollah link to the synagogue attack

On his Salem Radio Network broadcast, Marlow walked listeners through the background\. The attacker's brother, he said, was a Hezbollah operative killed during Israeli operations in Lebanon\. That death, Marlow explained, became the stated justification for targeting a Jewish house of worship in Michigan\.

Marlow put it bluntly:

> \"The terrorist brother apparently also was a Hezbollah terrorist who\.\.\.was killed by Israel in Lebanon\. So that's the backstory on this\. So that's why he's saying hurt people hurt people is because the guy's Hezbollah-tied brother died because of Israel\. Thus this is justified\.\"

Marlow's phrasing, \"Thus this is justified\", attributed that reasoning to El-Sayed's framing of the attack, not to Marlow himself\. The point was that El-Sayed's public comments treated a Hezbollah family connection and an act of anti-Jewish violence as something to be understood through a therapeutic lens, not condemned as terrorism with a clear ideological root\.

That distinction matters\. When a public figure responds to a synagogue attack by a man whose brother belonged to a U\.S\.-designated terrorist organization by reaching for the language of trauma counseling, the effect is to soften what should be a hard line\. The Democratic Party has faced growing warnings from within its own ranks about its posture toward Jewish voters and antisemitic violence\. El-Sayed's resurfaced comments fit squarely into that pattern\.

## Michigan's political class and the question nobody asked

What remains unanswered is almost as revealing as what the audio captured\. The S1 source does not name the specific attacker or the brother killed in Lebanon\. It does not detail charges, arrests, or the precise date of the synagogue attack\. Those gaps raise their own question: why has so little public attention been paid to the Hezbollah connection behind an attack on an American synagogue?

El-Sayed is not some anonymous commentator\. He is a Michigan political figure who ran for governor and has held public health positions in the state\. His willingness to frame a terrorist act as the predictable consequence of personal grief, rather than as ideologically motivated violence against Jews, reflects a broader pattern in progressive politics\. The instinct is always to contextualize, to explain, to redirect blame away from the actor and toward some larger systemic grievance\.

That instinct has consequences\. Jewish communities in Michigan and across the country have watched as elected officials and political aspirants treat attacks on synagogues with less moral clarity than they bring to far lesser offenses\. The internal fractures inside the Democratic Party over antisemitism and radical ideological drift are not abstract\. They show up in moments exactly like this one, when a resurfaced audio clip reveals what a political figure actually said when he thought the moment had passed\.

## No charges named, no condemnation offered

Marlow's broadcast did not detail the legal outcome of the synagogue attack, and the available reporting does not specify whether the attacker faced terrorism charges or was prosecuted under other statutes\. That absence is itself worth noting\. An attack on a synagogue by an individual with a direct family tie to Hezbollah, a group the U\.S\. government designates as a foreign terrorist organization, would seem to warrant the fullest possible legal response and the most unambiguous public condemnation\.

Instead, the public record includes audio of a prominent Michigan Democrat offering the attacker's perspective as though it were a reasonable frame\. \"Hurt people hurt people\" is a phrase borrowed from addiction recovery and childhood psychology\. Applying it to a man who targeted a Jewish congregation because Israel killed his Hezbollah-member brother is not compassion\. It is evasion\.

The broader political environment makes this worse, not better\. Democrats have faced sustained pressure over their handling of antisemitism, from campus protests to national security debates where the party's instincts have drawn bipartisan criticism\. Michigan, with its large and politically active Arab-American population, has become a flashpoint for these tensions\. El-Sayed's comments did not occur in a vacuum, they emerged from a political culture that treats ideological violence against Jews as a subject requiring nuance rather than condemnation\.

Republican voters in other states have shown they will hold their own party members accountable for failures of principle\. Louisiana GOP voters ousted a senator who broke with the party on a matter of conviction\. Whether Michigan Democrats will demand the same accountability from figures like El-Sayed remains an open question, though the early signs are not encouraging\.

## Audio doesn't lie, but silence speaks too

The resurfaced audio is damaging precisely because it is not a gaffe\. El-Sayed did not misspeak\. He offered a coherent framework for understanding why a man attacked a synagogue, and that framework treated the attacker's Hezbollah-connected grievance as the relevant context\. He did not call it terrorism\. He did not name the ideology\. He reached for empathy, directed not at the Jewish congregation that was targeted, but at the man who targeted them\.

Marlow's broadcast, airing coast to coast on Salem Radio Network and available as a podcast, brought the audio back into public view\. The question now is whether anyone in Michigan's political establishment will address it directly, or whether El-Sayed's framing will be allowed to stand as the last word from a Democratic figure on an act of anti-Jewish terrorism with ties to a designated terrorist organization\.

Concerns about election integrity and political accountability have driven investigations in other states, but the accountability gap in Michigan on this issue remains wide open\.

When a political figure's instinct after a synagogue attack is to explain the attacker rather than defend the attacked, voters deserve to know, and to remember\.
